narrative: The model estimates your chance of leaving at 47.0%. In this promotion review, that level of attrition risk was treated as too high: the organization denied the promotion because it expects you may soon depart. The most influential signal was your overall years of experience. With only 1–5 years across your career, you resemble about half of employees predicted to stay, and this factor pushed the decision toward staying. The second signal was that you reported other job opportunities while in this role. That is uncommon among employees predicted to stay—only about a quarter had such options—and it pushed strongly toward leaving. Third, your sector, classified as other, is less common among stayers than medical or education; this added further pressure toward leaving. Other profile details—overtime, unmet reward satisfaction, physical stress, and psychological exhaustion—may reinforce that concern, even if they were not the leading drivers. The organization should not treat this prediction as a final judgment. It should discuss your career path, promotion criteria, retention options, workload, and whether external opportunities make you likely to leave. You should ask what would change the decision and what support would keep you engaged.
